source_text: μέρους ἁγίαν καὶ ὑπὸ Θεῷ ζωήν· ἧς ὑποτύπωσις ἀκριβὴς, ἡ σεμίδαλις διὰ δρακὸς ἱερέως ἀναφερομένη σὺν τῷ ἐλαίῳ καὶ τῷ λιβάνῳ. Τὴν γάρ τοι Θεῷ καθιερουμένην ζωὴν, καὶ εἰ γένοιτο τυχὸν ἐκ μέρους, εὐώδη πάντως εἶναι χρὴ, καὶ λιπαρωτάταις ἐλπίσι πιαινομένην. Ἦ οὐκ εὐοσμότατον εἶναι φὴς πᾶν ἔργον ἡμῶν ἀγαθόν; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Τί δέ; οὐκ ἐπ' ἀγαθαῖς ἐλπίσι πράττεται πρὸς ἡμῶν; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ναί· ἕψεται γὰρ πάντως τὰ παρὰ Θεοῦ. {ΚΥΡ.} Λίβανος δὴ οὖν, καὶ σεμίδαλις ἐλαιόδευτος, τὴν εὐώδη τε καὶ λιπα
pass_a_gloss: §23 dual gloss: σεμίδαλις / fine flour; ἄζυμος / unleavened … Pass A scaffolding ≠ Pass B continuous English. Theme: Partial holy life = fine flour handful; unleavened; male priests eat;
pass_b_english: Cyril: …part holy and under God life; of which an accurate under-typing is the fine flour brought up through a priest’s handful with the oil and the frankincense. For the life being consecrated to God, even if it should somehow become from part, must be wholly fragrant, and being fattened with most rich hopes. Or do you not say every good work of ours is most sweet-smelling?
Cyril: And what? Is it not done by us upon good hopes?
Palladius: Yes; for the things from God will wholly follow.
Cyril: So then frankincense, and fine flour oil-wet, under-hints for us the fragrant and most rich life.
Palladius: You spoke well; but what would the as-from-part holy life become by us?

Cyril: The one neither having come unto a leaving-off of the sacred-fitting citizenship, nor going according to the very withdrawn path, of which sort somehow was John’s voice, or of the holy apostles; nor indeed falling out of being revered, through somehow having been worsted of the very underlying. Or is not the life of those in world and child-begetters, if they should choose to live through well, somehow shared to God and world, according to blessed Paul’s voice?
Palladius: It has been shared; for how not?

Cyril: So then a type of life not altogether dedicated to God, but as it were middle and looking upon both, was the partial consecration of the fine flour, having the fragrant and cheerful; which also the law says will be unto memorial of the one having brought through priestly service. And we will truly gain the lying in memory with God, through the things by which fruit-bearing we fragrance; with Christ mediating and bringing near to God, the one wholly holy, as in rank of the whole-burnt offerings; and indeed the one not such altogether through having been shared to the world, as it were some partial sacrifice. And unleavened is the sacrifice. For it would be fitting that everything whichever should become by us unto glory of God be done purely. And indeed the Savior has ordered to decline standing in mid markets making the prayers, and the unsmiling in fasts, and trumpeting disorderedly when pitying brothers. For this is leaven, profaning the sacred things. And what is done unto glory of God must have been released from charges of human-pleasing; for thus the victim would be truly unleavened and sacred. And portion and food for the priests is the leftover of the sacrifice. Every male is eaten in a holy place; the being spent of the sacred things in a holy place by the priests keeping reverence for our more mystical words; and the every male eating under-showing gracefully that softness is some unbeautiful thing and truly unholy for those chosen by God. For it finishes unhallowed, and sets out from spiritual blessing, and shows without share of the things from God apportioned to the saints (Leviticus 6:14–18) (1 Corinthians 7:32–34) (Matthew 6:2–6) (Matthew 6:16–18) (1 Corinthians 6:9–10)
